paragraphs: The paper studies how optimization can become faster when an algorithm uses information about the distribution of a problem’s curvature. It develops an average-case framework for random quadratic problems and derives algorithms that are optimal within that analysis. This makes the model of the Hessian’s eigenvalue distribution central to the acceleration strategy.

The authors provide explicit algorithms for uniform, Marchenko-Pastur, and exponential eigenvalue distributions. Although their design depends on this spectral information, their updates are simple: each uses the current gradient and the previous two iterates. Their momentum and step-size parameters can also be estimated without knowing the Hessian’s smallest singular value, a distinction the paper draws from classical accelerated methods.

Experiments cover quadratic problems and logistic regression. They identify regimes where these methods improve on classical acceleration designed around worst-case behavior. The finding is therefore conditional on the problem regime, rather than a claim of universal superiority. The contribution connects assumptions about the overall curvature distribution to practical, momentum-like optimization rules.
icml-2020-acceleration-through-spectral-.tldr: Modeling the Hessian’s eigenvalue distribution yields simple optimization methods with average-case acceleration and empirical advantages in some regimes.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures dependence between source text and generated target text. Methods that maximize it rely partly on a backward network, which models the source given the target. This paper argues that this backward direction deserves more attention because its quality affects how tightly the training objective bounds the mutual information being sought.

Adversarial Mutual Information organizes training as a min-max problem involving both forward and backward networks. By comparing real and generated data distributions, these networks can iteratively favor or discourage instances produced by each other. This makes their interaction part of the learning mechanism. The paper also introduces sampling of latent noise in a high-level semantic space to strengthen long-range dependencies during generation.

Across different text generation tasks, experiments show that the framework can significantly outperform several strong baselines. The authors also present evidence that it has the potential to tighten the variational lower bound used for mutual information maximization. That latter finding is a possibility supported by the work, rather than a guarantee that every trained model obtains a tighter bound.
icml-2020-adversarial-mutual-information.tldr: Adversarial training of forward and backward text models improves generation in experiments and may tighten a mutual-information lower bound.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning often needs substantial training data, making sample efficiency a practical concern. This paper asks whether expanding the representation of an agent’s observations can help it learn better policies. The question challenges the expectation that more input dimensions necessarily make learning harder.

The proposed online feature extractor, OFENet, uses a neural network to transform state observations into a higher-dimensional representation. That representation becomes the input to an off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm. The approach therefore changes what the policy-learning machinery receives, allowing it to work with learned features instead of relying directly on the lower-dimensional observations.

Numerical experiments show substantially better sample efficiency and performance with the proposed method. The authors suggest that stronger feature propagation and larger networks help agents learn more complex functions of state, offering an explanation for the improvement. This explanation is presented as their interpretation, while the direct finding is empirical: the learned, expanded representations helped in the experiments. The result supports investigating representation quality alongside input size when designing data-efficient agents.
icml-2020-can-increasing-input-dimension.tldr: OFENet expands state observations into learned features that improve reinforcement learning performance and sample efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: Structured prediction extends classification to outputs with internal organization, such as sequences or rankings. Existing max-margin Markov networks apply the support vector machine idea to this setting. The paper identifies a statistical problem with these methods when inputs do not nearly determine their labels: their learning objective can be inconsistent.

The authors replace the usual margin formulation with a max-min version, producing max-min margin Markov networks, or M4N. They prove consistency and finite-sample generalization bounds, and give an explicit algorithm for computing the estimator. These results connect the choice of training objective with both statistical reliability and an implementable learning procedure.

The algorithm achieves a generalization error rate of order one over the square root of the sample count using a number of projection-oracle calls linear in that count. Each call costs at most as much as the corresponding maximization oracle used by M3N. Experiments on multiclass classification, ordinal regression, sequence prediction, and ranking demonstrate effectiveness. Together, the results show that addressing inconsistency can be compatible with controlled computational cost.
icml-2020-consistent-structured-predicti.tldr: M4N replaces the structured max-margin objective with a max-min formulation that has consistency guarantees and an efficient learning algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much randomness a neural network needs to approximate a multidimensional distribution. It gives an explicit construction that starts with a single uniformly distributed noise variable and produces an arbitrarily close approximation to any two-dimensional target distribution satisfying the stated Lipschitz-continuity condition. Approximation quality is measured using Wasserstein distance.

The construction builds on a generalized space-filling property of sawtooth functions. This provides a concrete mechanism for transforming one-dimensional noise into a distribution that approximates a higher-dimensional target. The analysis highlights network depth as an important ingredient in making the Wasserstein error approach zero.

The authors also outline an extension to output distributions of arbitrary dimension. They show that the proposed construction incurs no additional Wasserstein-error cost relative to generating a d-dimensional target from d independent random variables. The comparison concerns approximation error in this distance. The result establishes a constructive representational capability: under the stated target conditions, low-dimensional input noise can support increasingly accurate distribution generation through a deep network.
icml-2020-constructive-universal-high-di.tldr: An explicit deep ReLU construction transforms one-dimensional uniform noise into arbitrarily accurate Wasserstein approximations of Lipschitz-continuous two-dimensional distributions.

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits support a broad range of exact, efficient inference operations. Yet their sparse computational connections can make implementations difficult to train on realistic datasets. This paper tackles that implementation bottleneck with Einsum Networks, or EiNets, aiming to make the existing probabilistic modeling framework more scalable.

The core design combines many arithmetic operations into one large einsum operation. This consolidates computation that would otherwise be spread across a sparsely connected graph. Compared with earlier implementations, the paper reports speed improvements and memory savings reaching two orders of magnitude. These are reported upper-end improvements, rather than a fixed gain for every use.

The authors also show how automatic differentiation can simplify implementing Expectation-Maximization for probabilistic circuits. Their experiments demonstrate scaling to datasets such as SVHN and CelebA, described as previously beyond reach, and show that EiNets can serve as faithful generative image models. The contribution links a computational redesign with a simpler training implementation, making tractable probabilistic models usable at larger data scales.
icml-2020-einsum-networks-fast-and-scala.tldr: EiNets consolidate probabilistic-circuit computation into einsum operations, substantially improving scalability while simplifying Expectation-Maximization training.

paragraphs: A linear autoencoder trained with mean squared reconstruction error can recover the principal subspace of the data’s sample covariance matrix. However, identifying that subspace does not identify its individual eigenvectors. The paper attributes this ambiguity to an invariance: changes inside the encoder and decoder can cancel in their combined mapping.

The authors introduce a loss that removes this ambiguity so that the decoder converges to the ordered, unnormalized eigenvectors of the sample covariance matrix. They analyze the entire loss landscape, providing an expression for all critical points and showing that these form a subset of the critical points of the conventional reconstruction loss.

The new landscape retains the property that every local minimum is global. The paper also shows how invariant global minima associated with the old objective become saddle points under the new one. Computing the loss and its gradients has the same complexity as mean squared error. This makes the change relevant to practical low-rank approximation as well as to understanding which representations an autoencoder’s objective identifies.
icml-2020-eliminating-the-invariance-on-.tldr: A new linear-autoencoder loss identifies ordered covariance eigenvectors while retaining globally optimal local minima and MSE-level computational complexity.

paragraphs: The Interferometric Graph Transform is a deep, unsupervised approach to learning graph representations. Its architecture works in a complex-valued spectral domain derived by generalizing the Euclidean Fourier transform. The paper uses this construction as the basis for a new class of graph convolutional neural networks.

A new greedy concave objective guides learning. The authors show that the resulting representation contains both discriminative and invariant features: it can preserve distinctions useful for distinguishing data while also capturing features that remain unchanged. Their experiments suggest that learning makes productive use of the spectral domain’s topology, which they describe as a usual weakness of spectral methods.

The evaluation spans image classification, community detection, and action recognition from videos of three-dimensional skeletons. The authors report state-of-the-art performance within the spectral graph unsupervised setting and show that the method can recover an analytic operator for vision tasks. These findings connect the spectral architecture and learning objective to several kinds of data, with the comparative performance claim specifically scoped to that unsupervised spectral setting.
icml-2020-interferometric-graph-transfor.tldr: IGT learns discriminative and invariant graph features through a complex-valued spectral architecture and a greedy concave objective.

paragraphs: Buchberger’s algorithm is central to studying exact solutions of polynomial systems, and optimized implementations matter for computer algebra software. This paper focuses on S-pair selection, a recurring choice within the algorithm. It investigates whether a reinforcement learning policy can make that choice in a way that reduces the amount of symbolic computation.

The authors study how problem difficulty changes with the domain and the distribution from which polynomials are drawn. They then train a policy using proximal policy optimization on random systems of binomial equations. Learning targets the selection strategy inside the existing algorithm, making a specific algorithmic decision the point of intervention.

In certain domains, the learned policy uses fewer total polynomial additions than state-of-the-art selection heuristics. That qualification matters: the reported advantage is domain-dependent and measured in polynomial additions. The result serves as a proof of concept that reinforcement learning can improve a component of a symbolic computation algorithm. It also emphasizes that the distribution of mathematical inputs is relevant when evaluating learned selection rules.
icml-2020-learning-selection-strategies-.tldr: A reinforcement learning policy reduces polynomial additions in Buchberger’s algorithm relative to leading selection heuristics in certain domains.

paragraphs: The paper proposes comparing reinforcement learning policies through their behaviors in a newly defined latent space. Wasserstein distance supplies the measure of difference between those behaviors. This gives policy optimization a way to account explicitly for behavioral similarity or separation when deciding how to improve a policy.

Using the dual formulation of Wasserstein distance, the method learns functions that assign scores to behaviors. Those scores can steer optimization toward desired behavior or away from undesired behavior. The authors combine this formulation with smoothed Wasserstein distances to build efficient algorithms that take stochastic gradient steps through the resulting regularization terms.

The framework leads to two on-policy methods: Behavior-Guided Policy Gradient and Behavior-Guided Evolution Strategies. Experiments show that these methods can outperform existing approaches across a variety of challenging environments. The contribution is both a comparison mechanism and a way to use that comparison during learning. Behavioral distance becomes an actionable training signal, with the reported performance advantages established empirically in the evaluated environments.
icml-2020-learning-to-score-behaviors-fo.tldr: Learned Wasserstein-based behavior scores guide policy optimization toward desired behaviors and away from undesired ones.

paragraphs: Structured prediction involves choosing among many possible organized outputs, such as trees or alignments. When that choice appears inside a neural network, training also requires gradients through the optimization step. SparseMAP addresses this with an interpretable combination of a few structures, but it depends on an exact maximum a posteriori inference oracle.

LP-SparseMAP extends that approach using a local polytope relaxation. This addresses the exact-inference requirement that prevents ordinary SparseMAP from handling models such as loopy graphical models or general logic constraints. Factor graphs provide the language for expressing the hidden structures, including hard logical rules, higher-order correlations, and coarse decompositions.

The paper derives both the forward computation and backward gradient algorithms needed to use LP-SparseMAP as a hidden or output layer. Experiments on three structured tasks show benefits over SparseMAP and Structured SVM. The central contribution is broader access to differentiable structured modeling: a relaxation makes more expressive constraints and interactions usable within a trainable layer, while retaining the sparse modeling approach.
icml-2020-lp-sparsemap-differentiable-re.tldr: LP-SparseMAP uses a local polytope relaxation to extend differentiable sparse structured prediction beyond models requiring exact MAP inference.

paragraphs: Recognizing a class from few examples is difficult when those examples do not cover changes in lighting, background, or shape. This paper proposes learning to share such variations across classes. The goal is to improve recognition of unseen examples without collecting a large set of varied observations for every target class.

The method uses meta-learning to transfer factors of variation from one class to another. These transferred variations produce virtual samples in the target class’s feature space during training. The augmented features simulate possible future query examples with similar changes, giving the model a broader range of training variation from a small number of actual examples.

The authors evaluate the approach on multiple benchmarks for few-shot classification and face recognition. They report significant improvements over the base model and performance exceeding relevant baselines. The findings support learning transferable variation as a way to strengthen recognition with scarce data. The mechanism operates through shared factors and feature-space augmentation, connecting experience from other classes to robustness on unseen examples and tasks.
icml-2020-meta-variance-transfer-learnin.tldr: Meta Variance Transfer augments scarce training examples by learning to transfer feature-space variations between classes.

paragraphs: Tensor latent factor models can capture higher-order relationships in spatial data, making them useful for spatial analysis. Their training can nevertheless be expensive and sensitive to initialization. Poor initialization can produce spatial patterns that lack coherence and are difficult to interpret. This paper addresses both the computational burden and the quality of the learned patterns.

Multiresolution Tensor Learning initializes its latent factors from an approximate full-rank tensor model. This is intended to improve interpretability. It then learns progressively from coarse spatial resolution to finer resolution, reducing computation by developing the model across levels of detail. The two choices address different parts of the problem: where training starts and how spatial detail enters the learning process.

The authors establish theoretical convergence and computational complexity results for the algorithm. On two real-world datasets, they report roughly four- to fivefold speedups over a fixed-resolution approach while obtaining accurate, interpretable latent factors. The findings indicate that progressive resolution can make spatial tensor learning faster while preserving useful, understandable patterns in the evaluated applications.
icml-2020-multiresolution-tensor-learnin.tldr: MRTL combines informed initialization with coarse-to-fine tensor learning to produce interpretable spatial factors with faster training in experiments.

paragraphs: Probabilistic clustering describes uncertainty over which cluster each observation belongs to. Computing that uncertainty can be slow or inaccurate because cluster assignments are discrete latent variables. This paper trains neural networks to generate approximate posterior samples of assignments, using labeled datasets sampled from a generative clustering model.

At test time, the networks handle new datasets of arbitrary size. The authors develop two complementary approaches: one needs a number of forward passes proportional to the number of observations, while the other needs passes proportional to the number of clusters. These counts describe how network evaluations scale with the dataset or its clustering.

Both approaches sample labels for all observations from a well-defined posterior. They also avoid fixing an upper limit on the number of mixture components, allowing them to learn nonparametric Bayesian posteriors. The paper presents neural spike sorting for high-density multielectrode arrays as a scientific application. Its contribution is a learned route to approximate clustering inference that accommodates variable dataset sizes and an unrestricted number of clusters.
icml-2020-neural-clustering-processes-1a.tldr: Neural Clustering Processes learn to sample approximate cluster-label posteriors for variable-size datasets without imposing a fixed limit on cluster count.

paragraphs: The paper introduces ParaNet, a fully convolutional model that converts text into a spectrogram without autoregressive generation. This changes the organization of synthesis so that the text-to-spectrogram stage can be computed in parallel. The authors report a 46.7-fold synthesis speedup over the lightweight Deep Voice 3 model while retaining reasonably good speech quality.

A second concern is aligning the input text with the generated speech. ParaNet improves attention progressively across layers, producing stable alignments on challenging test sentences. This layer-by-layer refinement provides a way to establish correspondence between text and speech within the non-autoregressive architecture.

The authors combine ParaNet with parallel neural vocoders to build systems that synthesize speech from text in a single feed-forward pass. They also explore a variational-autoencoder-based method for training an inverse autoregressive flow vocoder from scratch. That approach avoids requiring distillation from a separately trained WaveNet. Together, the contributions address parallel generation, stable alignment, and the training dependency of the waveform-generation component.
icml-2020-non-autoregressive-neural-text.tldr: ParaNet enables fast parallel text-to-spectrogram synthesis with stable alignments and combines with parallel vocoders for feed-forward speech generation.

paragraphs: The paper studies a generalization of determinantal point processes in which each subset receives weight from a product of matrix determinants. Turning these weights into probabilities requires a normalizing constant: the sum of the weights over all subsets. The authors investigate how difficult this essential inference calculation is.

Their results establish strong computational barriers. Exactly summing fixed positive even powers of principal-minor determinants is UP-hard and Mod3P-hard. For products involving three matrices, even approximation within the stated factor is NP-hard; that factor grows as two raised to a power of the input size. These complexity results largely rule out efficient general-purpose solutions under the corresponding complexity assumptions.

The paper also identifies favorable structure that enables computation for products involving two matrices. An algorithm runs in k raised to order k times a polynomial in input size, where k can be the maximum matrix rank or the treewidth of the combined nonzero-entry graph. Thus, small structural parameters offer a tractable route even though unrestricted instances face substantial complexity barriers.
icml-2020-on-the-in-tractability-of-comp.tldr: Normalizing products of determinantal point processes faces strong complexity barriers, but small rank or treewidth enables parameterized algorithms for two matrices.

paragraphs: A prediction can affect the decisions people make and thereby change the outcome being predicted. The paper calls this performative prediction. If a learning system ignores that feedback, the resulting changes can appear as distribution shift, prompting retraining without explicitly accounting for how the model helped create the new data.

The authors develop a risk-minimization framework that combines ideas from statistics, game theory, and causality. Its central equilibrium concept is performative stability. At such a point, predictions are calibrated against the future outcomes produced by acting on those predictions. This shifts attention from fitting a historical distribution to the relationship between a deployed predictor and the outcomes it induces.

The main results give necessary and sufficient conditions for retraining to converge to a performatively stable point with nearly minimal loss. These are conditional convergence results, so retraining is not asserted to succeed under arbitrary feedback. The framework also strictly includes strategic classification, and the paper supplies sufficient conditions under which retraining can overcome strategic feedback effects.
icml-2020-performative-prediction-cd3fe8.tldr: Performative prediction formalizes how deployed predictions change outcomes and establishes conditions for retraining to reach a stable, nearly optimal predictor.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of two sparse linear models whose outputs are mixed together. Each label comes from one of the models, so the observations combine two different input-output relationships. This is a simple model of heterogeneous data, where a single linear rule is insufficient to describe all responses.

The setting allows experimental design: the learner chooses feature vectors and queries an oracle for their labels. For each query, the oracle randomly selects one of the two sparse models and generates the response. The task is to recover both models simultaneously, and the central question is how many oracle queries this requires.

The authors provide efficient recovery algorithms that improve on previously known query-complexity results. They frame the problem as a generalization of compressed sensing, extending sparse recovery to measurements drawn from a mixture of two linear sources. The ability to design and query features is a stated part of the setting. The contribution therefore concerns efficient recovery under that query access, with the number of measurements as the main resource being improved.
icml-2020-recovery-of-sparse-signals-fro.tldr: Efficient algorithms improve query complexity for recovering two sparse linear models from designed measurements whose generating model is randomly selected.

paragraphs: The paper examines estimating a fixed policy’s value function with TD(0) from a batch of observations. It identifies a source of error: actions influence updates according to how often they appear in the batch. Those empirical frequencies can differ from the action probabilities specified by the policy being evaluated.

Policy sampling error corrected TD(0), or PSEC-TD(0), estimates the batch’s action distribution separately for each state. It then applies importance sampling to correct the mismatch between empirical frequencies and policy probabilities. This targets the weighting of updates following actions, addressing a reason ordinary batch TD(0) may converge to an inaccurate value estimate.

The authors refine the notion of a certainty-equivalence estimate and argue that their correction uses a fixed batch more efficiently. Evaluations on three value-function learning tasks, including analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity, find lower mean squared error than TD(0). The results show that correcting action-frequency discrepancies can improve estimates from already collected data, with the empirical advantage established on the tasks studied.
icml-2020-reducing-sampling-error-in-bat.tldr: PSEC-TD(0) corrects mismatches between observed action frequencies and policy probabilities, lowering value-estimation error in batch-learning experiments.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares distributions using a ground cost that specifies how costly it is to move mass between points. Regularization has helped make these problems practical for machine learning. Entropy regularization, for example, supports faster computation and differentiation through the Sinkhorn algorithm, along with improved sample-complexity bounds.

This paper develops a different interpretation of regularization: robustness to adversarial choices of the ground cost. Using Fenchel duality, the authors show that any convex regularization of optimal transport admits this ground-cost-adversarial interpretation. The convexity qualification defines the scope of the stated result. The contribution gives an alternative mathematical meaning to modifying the transport objective.

The interpretation also yields a robust dissimilarity measure on the underlying space of points. The authors propose algorithms for computing this robust cost and illustrate the approach empirically. That makes the result more than a reinterpretation of an existing calculation: it provides a cost measure that can be used in other applications. The work links regularized distribution comparison with robustness in the pointwise costs that comparison uses.
icml-2020-regularized-optimal-transport-.tldr: Convex regularization of optimal transport can be interpreted as adversarial modification of the ground cost, yielding a computable robust dissimilarity.

paragraphs: Disentanglement aims to separate factors of variation so that representations are understandable and generation is controllable. This paper addresses difficulties with high-resolution images, the emphasis of earlier work on representations, and the non-identifiability associated with unsupervised learning. It introduces StyleGAN-based architectures and losses that use limited supervision.

To evaluate the approach systematically, the authors create two complex synthetic datasets with high-resolution images and also investigate real data. They report good disentanglement with very small labeled fractions, giving figures of 0.25% and 2.5%. This provides empirical evidence that limited supervision can be sufficient in their studied settings, without establishing a universal labeling requirement.

The paper introduces metrics for measuring how controllable a generator is. Its observations suggest a potentially important trade-off between learning disentangled representations and achieving controllable generation. Those goals therefore need separate evaluation rather than being assumed to improve together. The authors also consider fine-grained semantic image editing to improve generalization to unseen images, connecting the representation-learning work to control over new image inputs.
icml-2020-semi-supervised-stylegan-for-d.tldr: Semi-supervised StyleGAN learns disentanglement with few labels and reveals a possible trade-off between representation disentanglement and generator controllability.

paragraphs: Transformers can combine information over long time horizons, making them appealing for reinforcement learning when an agent cannot fully observe its environment. However, the paper finds that the standard architecture is difficult to optimize with reinforcement learning objectives. Its potential for memory therefore comes with a substantial training challenge.

The authors propose architectural changes that improve the stability and learning speed of both the original Transformer and its XL variant. The resulting Gated Transformer-XL, or GTrXL, is designed to make that sequence-modeling capacity more usable in reinforcement learning. The intervention addresses the architecture through which learning occurs.

GTrXL surpasses LSTMs on challenging memory environments and achieves state-of-the-art results on the multitask DMLab-30 benchmark, exceeding an external-memory architecture. The authors also find stability and performance that consistently match or exceed a competitive LSTM baseline, including on more reactive tasks where memory matters less. These experiments support the architectural changes across both memory-demanding settings and tasks with less need for long-term information.
icml-2020-stabilizing-transformers-for-r.tldr: GTrXL modifies Transformers to improve reinforcement learning stability and speed, with strong results on memory-intensive and reactive tasks.

paragraphs: Linear quadratic regulation offers a well-established framework for continuous control. This paper asks how to learn a linear controller with additional structure, such as sparsity, block sparsity, or low rank. Such structure can make a policy easier to interpret, reduce its memory requirements, and support distributed use.

The authors formulate a regularized LQR problem when the system model is known. Structured Policy Iteration alternates policy evaluation with policy improvement to solve this problem efficiently. They also extend the algorithm to the model-free setting, using a smoothing procedure to estimate the gradient when direct access to the model is unavailable.

Convergence analyses cover both settings under appropriate parameter choices. This condition is part of the guarantee. Experiments vary the regularization weight to demonstrate how the method balances control performance against the degree of policy structure. The contribution gives a systematic way to pursue structured controllers while exposing that balance, rather than treating sparsity or low rank as a separate property added after optimizing control performance.
icml-2020-structured-policy-iteration-fo.tldr: Structured Policy Iteration learns sparse or low-rank LQR controllers, with conditional convergence guarantees in known-model and model-free settings.

paragraphs: Supervised learning requires choosing a loss function, yet that choice is often made informally among many theoretically acceptable options. This paper develops a principled way to learn the loss alongside a classifier. It starts by reinterpreting SLIsotron as selecting a loss from a family of composite square losses.

Through the theory of proper losses, the authors generalize that interpretation using Bregman divergences. The resulting BregmanTron algorithm jointly learns the classifier and its loss. It includes a convergence guarantee for the learned loss, and its possible outputs have a guarantee of agnostic approximability of the Bayes rule. These theoretical properties support the approach beyond its experimental performance.

Experiments indicate that BregmanTron significantly outperforms SLIsotron. They also show that other algorithms can minimize the learned loss for different tasks. This suggests the possibility of transferring a learned loss between domains, which the authors identify as a further research problem. The contribution treats the training criterion itself as a learnable object with theoretical structure and potential reuse.
icml-2020-supervised-learning-no-loss-no.tldr: BregmanTron jointly learns a classifier and its loss, combining theoretical guarantees with empirical gains and evidence for possible loss transfer.

paragraphs: T-Basis provides a compact way to represent a collection of tensors, the multidimensional arrays used in neural networks. The tensors in that collection can have different shapes. The approach represents each tensor using a Tensor Ring, giving the collection a structure that can be described through smaller components.

The central idea is to use a shared list of three-dimensional tensors, all with the same shape, to represent the nodes of those Tensor Rings. This list is the T-Basis. Coefficients associated with its tensors provide a compact parameterization of the collection. The authors also state that the concept applies to other Tensor Networks.

The number of coefficients scales logarithmically with each represented tensor’s size and linearly with the dimensionality of the T-Basis. In neural network compression experiments, the method achieves high compression with performance decreases the authors describe as acceptable. Their analysis of memory and operation requirements further supports their conclusion that T-Basis networks are suited to both training and inference under resource constraints, including use on edge devices.
icml-2020-t-basis-a-compact-representati.tldr: T-Basis compactly represents neural network tensors through shared Tensor Ring components, achieving high compression with performance drops the authors describe as acceptable.
